exploration.title: Caravan Crossroads
exploration.subject: History
exploration.summary: Predict, then compare how changing only season or route affects travel time, delivered cargo, load and margin in a fictional trade model.
exploration.question: When every other rule stays fixed, how can one modeled route or season change alter several journey outcomes?
exploration.explanation: The historical Silk Roads were overlapping land and sea networks connecting many communities, not one road or a one-way end-to-end journey. Goods, knowledge, skills and ideas moved through local and long-distance exchanges, often changing hands between merchants. This lesson studies two controlled comparisons on one fictional composite segment. Every location, duration, season effect, carrying limit, price, toll, margin, spoilage rule and breakage rule is a teaching assumption, not a historical measurement, probability or forecast.

experiments.title: Change only the season
experiments.instruction: Keep River Road, 6 grain units, 14 supply days, the 100 kg limit and all price and loss rules fixed. Predict whether changing wet season to dry creates more, the same or fewer travel days, then compare the two plans.
experiments.observe: Wet to dry changes 8 to 14 days and 6 to 4 units delivered, while load stays 64 kg. Margin changes from −8 to −22 teaching credits because the invented dry-season rule adds time and crosses the invented grain-spoilage threshold.

experiments.title: Change only the route
experiments.instruction: Keep dry season, 6 pottery units, 12 supply days, the 100 kg limit and all price and loss rules fixed. Predict whether Mountain Pass, Oasis Trail or neither delivers more pottery and keeps the larger margin, then compare.
experiments.observe: Mountain Pass takes 9 days, delivers 5 units and has margin 0. Oasis Trail takes 12 days, delivers 6 units and has margin 15 teaching credits. Both loads stay 66 kg; the longer fictional route avoids the invented breakage rule and has the lower invented toll.

exploration.misconception: The Silk Roads were not one road, a simple east-to-west line or a route where the same merchant usually carried goods end to end. Many communities, local exchanges and changing land and sea routes formed the networks.
